21929-a-master-of-craft:
A pretty girl stands on a Wapping jetty at evening in W. W. Jacobs's novel A Master of Craft, published in 1899. Below her rests the schooner Foam, her galley cold and her hatches closed against the quiet Thames. The girl puts a small foot toward the rigging, thinking of the jump down. She wants Captain Flower, who went ashore half an hour before.

A young man hurries up, and the tale of the Foam begins. Jacobs stretches his short-story gifts across a full novel of sailors, courtship, and craft. Fraser, in the talk quoted at the front, wonders why the captain never mentioned the girl's dark eyes. The master of craft of the title has more to master than his ship. It is Jacobs afloat and ashore at once.
22800-mary-wollstonecraft:
Mary Wollstonecraft is a biography of the great feminist pioneer, published in 1884, when her reputation still needed rescue. The catalog record names no author. Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, had been dead nearly ninety years, and respectable opinion still treated her life as a scandal.

Few women, the biographer begins, worked so faithfully for humanity's cause. Few drew such bitter censure, either. She gave herself to relieving suffering fellow beings with a saint's ardor. In return, people called her a moral scourge of God. The biography argues her case with documents and sympathy. It stands near the head of the long effort that restored Wollstonecraft to her place in history.
22822-the-superstitions-of-witchcraft:
Howard Williams, a scholar with an M.A., surveys the long history of witchcraft belief in The Superstitions of Witchcraft. Dreams, magic terrors, miracles, witches, ghosts, and portents all crowd his opening pages. Williams stresses that such fears were not confined to remote ages or to the so-called dark ages of Europe.

He finds the clearest proof much closer to his own time. The laws, theology, and popular prejudice of the seventeenth century supply case after case of accusation and punishment. By tracing how educated people endorsed the panic, Williams turns a lurid subject into social history. The book suits readers who want the witch trials explained as a product of belief, law, and fear together.
